book.title: Sefer Soḳolḳah = Dos bukh fun Soḳolḳe (ʻa.y. Irgun Yotsʼe Soḳolḳah be-Yiśraʼel)

overview.title: Jewish Sokółka through Sefer Sokolkah
overview.summary: Sokółka was a Jewish community shaped by religious learning, Hebrew and Yiddish culture, schools, trades, family networks, and increasingly varied political movements. The memorial book follows this life from earlier communal history and the vibrant interwar years through wartime occupation, ghettoization, deportation, murder, escape, and the difficult survival of individuals. It also preserves accounts of survivors, emigrants, and descendants who carried Sokółka’s memory beyond the town. By exploring these paths, readers can see both the institutions that sustained the community and the human consequences of its destruction.

paths.title: What kind of Jewish community was Sokółka?
paths.description: This path introduces Sokółka as a lived community rather than only a place later destroyed. By the end, readers will understand how commerce, family, charity, civic organization, and shared customs structured everyday Jewish life.
paths.question: How did Jewish residents build a community and make a life in Sokółka?

steps.title: A community with deep roots
steps.summary: The memorial book presents Sokółka as a Jewish community connected historically with Grodno and records a privilege granted to Sokółka’s Jews in 1698. It also describes Jewish residents as central to local commerce, industry, and crafts, showing that community life was tied to both communal belonging and economic activity.

paths.title: How did Sokółka’s Jews educate and express themselves?
paths.description: This path follows the community’s religious schools, Hebrew education, youth culture, newspapers, theater, and music. It shows how education and culture connected tradition with modern Jewish identities and public life.
paths.question: What did children and young people learn, read, perform, and imagine in Sokółka?

steps.summary: The Talmud Torah served most children in the city and surrounding area before the First World War, while another account describes free study for poor boys in the synagogue courtyard. paths.title: How did tradition and modern Jewish politics coexist?
paths.description: This path examines rabbis, religious learning, Zionism, Mizrachi, and youth activism without reducing Sokółka to a single ideology. Readers will see a community in which religious authority and political experimentation operated alongside one another.
paths.question: How did Sokółka’s Jews debate Jewish identity, responsibility, and the future?

steps.title: Rabbis and religious authority
steps.summary: Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Director served as Sokółka’s rabbi from 1883 to 1900, and the book also remembers Rabbi Israel Goldin’s study, service, sermons, and later rabbinic career. Their biographies show religious leadership as an important part of the community’s public and intellectual life.

paths.title: What happened to Sokółka under occupation?
paths.description: This path traces the transition from invasion and persecution to ghetto confinement, forced labor, deportation, and murder. It emphasizes the sequence recorded by survivors and memorial-book testimonies while preserving uncertainty where the accounts themselves are approximate.
paths.question: How did occupation dismantle Jewish life in Sokółka?

steps.title: War and changing rulers
steps.summary: The book recalls the outbreak of the Second World War in September 1939, German entry, and the subsequent arrival of Soviet forces. A second German occupation began in 1941, after which persecution of Jews intensified.

paths.title: Who survived, and how?
paths.description: This path follows the narrow and dangerous possibilities of escape, hiding, rescue, work, and return. It also shows why survival stories must be read alongside the overwhelming destruction recorded in the same memorial book.
paths.question: What forms of survival and resistance appear in the Sokółka testimonies?

paths.title: How was Sokółka remembered after the catastrophe?
paths.description: This path treats Sefer Sokolkah as an act of remembrance assembled from biographies, testimonies, lists, photographs, and communal initiatives. Readers will understand how survivors and descendants preserved names, relationships, institutions, and aspirations that persecution sought to erase.
paths.question: How did survivors and descendants keep Sokółka present after the war?

timeline.title: A privilege for Sokółka’s Jews
timeline.summary: The memorial book records Augustus II issuing a privilege to the Jews of Sokółka. This places Jewish communal rights within the town’s earlier recorded history.

timeline.title: Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Director serves Sokółka
timeline.summary: Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Director served as rabbi of Sokółka during these years. The book also remembers his rabbinical writing and communal religious authority.

timeline.title: Welfare organization and a devastating fire
timeline.summary: A local welfare office was established in 1888; the following year, a fire destroyed sixty houses and left sixty families destitute. The book records communal organization alongside vulnerability to disaster.

timeline.title: Zionist organization grows
timeline.summary: Sokółka Zionists supported Jewish agricultural workers in Palestine and participated in regional Zionist activity, including a 1900 conference. The book presents this as a significant strand of public communal life.

records.summary: About three hundred community members formed an association supporting Jewish agricultural workers in Palestine.

timeline.title: Religious Zionism and Hebrew schooling
timeline.summary: A Mizrachi branch was established in Sokółka in 1902, followed by the opening of a reformed school and the founding of a Hebrew school in 1903–1904. These developments joined religious politics with educational renewal.

timeline.dateLabel: First World War and its aftermath
timeline.title: War brings occupation and displacement
timeline.summary: The book recalls German arrival in 1914, the movement of one family from Białystok to Sokółka, German capture of Sokółka in 1915, and the end of German rule in 1918. These accounts show how war reshaped local lives and political control.

records.title: German arrival in 1914
records.summary: The Germans arrived in 1914, according to the passage.
records.quote: אי ן יא ר 1914 קומע ן ד י דייטשן .

records.title: Move to Sokolka
records.summary: The narrator’s family moved from Bialystok to Sokolka during the First World War.
records.quote: או ן מי ר זיינע ן געוואר ן סאקאלקע ר תושבים

records.title: German capture of Sokolka
records.summary: German forces entered and captured Sokolka in 1915.
records.quote: ב- 1915 נכבש ה סוקולק ה ביד י הצב א הגרמנ י

records.title: End of German rule in occupied territories
records.summary: German rule ended in occupied territories in 1918 amid revolution and Polish independence efforts.
records.quote: בשנ ת 1918 הגי ע קיצ ו ש ל השלטו ן הגרמנ י בשטח י הכבוש

timeline.title: Pioneering, education, and new movements
timeline.summary: HeHalutz arose in Sokółka in 1919–1920, Tarbut classes were photographed in 1927, and Freiheit organized in the late 1920s. The period reflects continued political, educational, and youth activity after the First World War.

records.quote: בשנו ת 1920 ־ 1919 קמ ה תנוע ת "החלוץ"

timeline.title: Cultural creativity and organized youth life
timeline.summary: In 1932, a seventeen-year-old assembled Sokółka’s first and only radio program, while a HeHalutz membership committee was established in 1938. These records suggest continuing local initiative shortly before the Second World War.

records.title: Radio program invention
records.summary: Bezalel Kruglik invented and assembled Sokolka’s first and only radio program at age seventeen, according to a 1932 newspaper article.
records.quote: ב ן 17 , ע ם תכני ת הרדי ו שהמצי א והרכיב

timeline.title: The Second World War reaches Sokółka
timeline.summary: The memorial-book accounts recall the outbreak of war on September 1, German entry, and the subsequent arrival of Soviet forces. The change of occupying power began a new period of uncertainty for the town’s Jews.

records.title: Outbreak of the Second World War in Sokolka
records.summary: War began, followed by mobilization and German reconnaissance over Sokolka.
records.quote: בפרו ץ מלחמ ת העול ם השני ה ב־ 1.9.1939

records.title: German invasion of Sokółka
records.summary: German forces invaded Sokółka shortly before or during the beginning of World War II.

records.summary: Soviet forces entered Sokolka after the German entry in 1939.

timeline.title: Second German occupation and ghettoization
timeline.summary: German forces returned in 1941, persecution began, and Jewish residents were ordered into the ghetto during Sukkot. The ghetto’s gate and police guard hut were located on Białystok Street.

records.title: Second German occupation of Sokolka
records.summary: German forces invaded after bombing the airfield and established a military camp.
records.quote: ב . הכבו ש השנ י ש ל הגרמני ם 1941

records.quote: ניתנד , הפקודד , לעבו ר לגיטו

timeline.title: Transfers, selections, and escape
timeline.summary: Most Jews were transferred from the ghetto to Kolbasin after 1942, followed by a November selection and transfer toward a work location. Abraham Kantarowski’s testimony records an escape from the ghetto in November.

timeline.title: Deportation to Auschwitz
timeline.summary: The remaining ghetto prisoners were deported toward Auschwitz in January, while approximately four hundred factory workers were deported on January 23. The book reports that most arrivals were murdered and burned on January 25, with six factory workers surviving.

records.quote: ב־ 18 בינוא ר ניתנ ה הפקודה : "יודענריין"

records.title: Factory workers deported to Auschwitz
records.summary: On January 23, 1943, 400 men from the factory were deported to Auschwitz; six survived.

timeline.title: The destruction reaches Białystok
timeline.summary: The final Białystok aktion took place on August 16, 1943. The memorial book reports that approximately two thousand Jews were burned alive, including Zindel Chinski from Sokółka.

records.quote: ביו ם 16 באוגוס ט 1943

timeline.title: Liberation and Soviet capture
timeline.summary: Radio announcements reported liberated towns in summer 1944, and Soviet forces captured Sokółka in 1945 after German withdrawal. These events mark the end of German control, not the restoration of the destroyed prewar community.

records.summary: Radio announcements reported liberation of Grodno and other towns during summer 1944.

timeline.title: Survivors move through a changed world
timeline.summary: A survivor traveled toward Sokółka in July 1946, while another narrator reached Israel with her child in December 1949. The book records postwar movement and resettlement alongside the deaths and absences left by the war.

records.title: Return toward Sokółka

records.quote: מי ר פאר ן צוזאמע ן דע ם 7 יול י 1946

timeline.title: Organized remembrance continues
timeline.summary: A society meeting in 1959 recorded a contribution decision, and the book later records the death of educator Penina Kantor in 1963. These entries belong to the continuing postwar work of community and memory.
